snippet.title: Why Does Diesel Fuel Have So Many Different Colors in America? 😳
snippet.description:
Why Does Diesel Fuel Have So Many Different Colors in America? 😳

Why are there so many different colors of diesel fuel in the United States? Can you tell how good the diesel is just by looking at its color?
Actually, no. These colors are not used to indicate the fuel's quality or performance. Instead, they help identify what the fuel is intended for and whether it is subject to certain taxes.
One of the most important types is Red Diesel. It is mainly used in tractors, harvesters, and other off-road machinery. Since these machines generally don't travel on public roads, red diesel can be sold tax-free under certain regulations. On the other hand, clear or pale yellow diesel is used in regular trucks and other road vehicles. It already includes the applicable road fuel taxes. Now, what about Blue Diesel? It was previously used to identify certain types of off-road diesel. However, today, you cannot determine whether the fuel is tax-exempt just by looking at its color. Green and purple diesel also have no single standardized legal meaning across the United States. Their significance depends on local regulations and how fuel suppliers label their products. So, the color of diesel doesn't tell you about its quality. Instead, it helps identify what the fuel is meant to be used for and whether certain taxes apply. Do you think other countries should also adopt different fuel colors to identify tax-exempt diesel?

Fuel color alone does not determine its quality, tax status, or legal eligibility. Always check local regulations and official fuel specifications before using any type of diesel.

Only one country makes it overflow: Russia. Its European part alone, west of the Urals, is almost 4 million km², and that tips the total to about 116% of Brazil.

The tune is Ode to Joy, the EU's anthem, played as a samba.

Sources: CIA World Factbook, IBGE, Natural Earth
